transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

Well, I guess what brings me in is that I've been taking on way too much lately. I got involved with this historical society project, and... I just kind of took it on like I could run the whole fundraiser by myself. I started drawing up all these new quilt designs, calling up volunteers, making schedules, and just promising people deadlines that I couldn't possibly meet. It just got totally out of hand.
During this time, have you felt unusually high or euphoric?

Well, yes, I did. At first, I felt almost... glowing, I guess you could say. It was like every single idea I had was just wonderful. But, um, if anyone questioned me about the plans, I got really snappish. I just acted like they were standing in the way.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when you felt depressed or lost interest in things most of the day nearly every day?

Yes, I have. Actually, that's kind of where I'm at right now. I used to really love going out and checking my garden every day, and working on my own quilt entries. But lately... I don't know, I just look at the fabric and the seed catalogs when they come in the mail, and I feel nothing much at all. I just don't have any interest in doing any of it.
During that high period, did you have any experiences like hearing or seeing things other people didn’t, or strongly believing something that others said wasn’t true?

No, nothing like that. I didn't hear voices or see anything that wasn't there. And I didn't have any strange beliefs... I just thought I could do a lot more than I actually could. But I never lost touch with reality or anything.
About how many days in a row did that unusually high-energy period last?

Well, it was a lot longer than just a few days. That whole overdriven stretch... um, I was working on a big project for the historical society at the time. It went on for about five months straight before everything finally fell apart.

final_diagnosis.reason: The interview supports bipolar affective disorder with a current hypomanic/manic-spectrum episode without psychotic symptoms and a history of a depressive episode. The patient describes a distinct prolonged period of elevated mood, increased goal-directed activity, overcommitment, grandiose overestimation of abilities, and irritability, followed by a current depressive episode with anhedonia. Psychotic symptoms were explicitly denied. Given the provided candidate set, F31.1 is the best-fitting ICD-10 diagnosis.
